question: Duke OIT will perform scheduled maintenance on the campus VPN service on Saturday, March 14, from 6:00 AM to 10:00 AM. During this window, Cisco AnyConnect connections to vpn.duke.edu may be intermittently unavailable, and active sessions could be disconnected without warning. Users who rely on the VPN for off-campus access to restricted systems, including the library's licensed databases and departmental file shares, should plan to complete time-sensitive work outside the maintenance window. No action is required from end users; existing client software will reconnect automatically once the service is restored. Questions can be directed to the OIT Service Desk at 919-684-2200.
reference: Duke's campus VPN (vpn.duke.edu via Cisco AnyConnect) has scheduled maintenance Saturday March 14, 6-10 AM, during which connections may drop intermittently. Users needing off-campus access to restricted systems should work outside that window; no user action is needed since clients reconnect automatically. Contact the OIT Service Desk (919-684-2200) with questions.

question: Under Duke's data classification policy, university data is grouped into three sensitivity levels: Public, Sensitive, and Restricted. Public data may be freely shared and carries no handling requirements. Sensitive data — which includes most student education records and non-public operational information — must be stored only in Duke-approved services such as Duke Box or Duke OneDrive and may not be placed in personal cloud accounts. Restricted data, the highest tier, covers information whose disclosure could cause significant harm, such as Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, and protected health information; it requires encryption in transit and at rest and is subject to additional access controls. When a dataset combines multiple elements, it inherits the classification of its most sensitive component.
reference: Duke classifies data as Public, Sensitive, or Restricted. Public data has no handling rules; Sensitive data (e.g., most student records) must stay in approved services like Box or OneDrive, not personal accounts; Restricted data (SSNs, financial accounts, PHI) additionally requires encryption and extra access controls. A mixed dataset takes the classification of its most sensitive element.

question: The Duke Compute Cluster (DCC) is a shared high-performance computing environment available to Duke researchers. Jobs are submitted through the Slurm scheduler rather than run interactively on login nodes, which are reserved for editing, compiling, and lightweight tasks. Each research group is allocated storage under /work, while home directories are limited to 25 GB and are not intended for large datasets. Free, lower-priority access is available to all users through the common partition, and groups that have purchased dedicated nodes receive higher scheduling priority on their own partitions. Users running large or long jobs should request appropriate resources in their submission scripts; jobs that exceed requested memory or time limits are terminated by the scheduler.
reference: The Duke Compute Cluster is a shared HPC system where work is submitted via the Slurm scheduler (login nodes are only for light tasks like editing/compiling). Storage lives under /work per group; home directories are capped at 25 GB. All users get free low-priority access on the common partition, while groups owning nodes get higher priority; jobs exceeding requested memory or time are killed.

question: Duke University Libraries has expanded access to its interlibrary loan service for the upcoming semester. Students, faculty, and staff can now request articles and book chapters not held in Duke's collections at no cost, with most digital articles delivered within 24 to 48 hours directly to the requester's email. Physical books borrowed from partner institutions typically arrive within one to two weeks and can be picked up at Perkins Library or, on request, routed to the Ford Library or the Marine Lab. The service is accessed through the library website using NetID login. There is no limit on the number of requests, though the library asks that users cancel requests they no longer need so that resources can be redirected.
reference: Duke Libraries' interlibrary loan now provides free article and book-chapter requests for students, faculty, and staff, with most digital articles emailed within 24-48 hours and physical books from partner libraries arriving in 1-2 weeks for pickup at Perkins (or Ford/Marine Lab on request). Access it via the library website with NetID; there's no request limit, but users should cancel ones they no longer need.

question: The Office of Information Technology has issued a security advisory following a rise in targeted phishing emails aimed at Duke community members. The recent messages impersonate Duke departments and ask recipients to log in through a linked page to 'verify' their account or review a shared document; the linked pages closely mimic the real Duke single sign-on screen. OIT reminds users that Duke will never ask for a NetID password by email and that legitimate logins always occur at the official shib.oit.duke.edu address. Recipients who receive a suspicious message should not click any links, should report it using the 'Report Phishing' button in Outlook, and should change their NetID password immediately if they entered credentials. Enabling Duo multifactor authentication significantly reduces the risk that a stolen password alone can compromise an account.
reference: OIT warns of increased phishing emails impersonating Duke departments and linking to fake single sign-on pages to steal credentials. Duke never requests NetID passwords by email, and real logins happen at shib.oit.duke.edu. Don't click links; report suspicious mail via Outlook's 'Report Phishing' button, and change your password immediately if you entered it. Duo MFA greatly reduces the damage a stolen password can do.

question: Beginning this fall, Duke is updating its policy on the use of generative AI tools in coursework. The policy establishes that individual instructors set the rules for their own courses and must state those rules clearly in the syllabus; in the absence of an explicit statement, students should assume that unauthorized use of AI tools to complete graded work is not permitted. The policy distinguishes between using AI as a permitted study aid and submitting AI-generated work as one's own, the latter of which may constitute a violation of the Duke Community Standard. Faculty are encouraged to discuss expectations with students early in the term and to design assessments that make the intended role of AI tools explicit. Questions about academic integrity can be directed to the Office of Student Conduct.
reference: Duke's updated generative-AI coursework policy puts each instructor in charge of their own course's rules, which must be stated in the syllabus; absent a statement, students should assume unauthorized AI use on graded work is not allowed. It separates AI as a permitted study aid from submitting AI work as one's own (a possible Community Standard violation). Faculty should set expectations early; academic-integrity questions go to the Office of Student Conduct.
